'''David Edward Hugh Jones''' (20 April 1938 – 19 July 2017) was a British chemist and writer, who - under the pen name Daedalus - was the fictional inventor for DREADCO.  Jones' columns as Daedalus were published for 38 years, starting weekly in 1964 in ''[[New Scientist]]''. He then moved to the journal ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', and continued to publish until 2002.  Columns from these magazines, along with additional comments and implementation sketches, were collected in two books: ''The Inventions of Daedalus:  A Compendium of Plausible Schemes'' (1982) and ''The Further Inventions of Daedalus'' (1999).

==Early life and education==

He was born in [[Southwark]], London. His father, Philip, was an advertising copywriter. His mother was Dorothea, née Sitters. He had one brother, [[Peter Jones (classicist)|Peter Vaughan Jones]].<ref name="NYT">{{cite news
|title=David E.H. Jones, Scientist Whose Alter Ego Challenged Conventions, Dies at 79
|work=The New York Times
|author=Sam Roberts
|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/07/30/science/david-joins-dead-wrote-science-columns-as-daedalus.html
|date=30 July 2017
|access-date=1 August 2017
}}</ref> He attended Crofton Primary School in Orpington, Kent, and then [[Eltham College]].<ref name="Times">{{cite journal
|journal=The Times
|title=Obituaries
|date=7 August 2017
|page=41 |url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/science/article/obituary-david-jones-svktlclv2
}}</ref>

His professional training was as a chemist. In 1962, he graduated in chemistry and completed a PhD in organic chemistry from [[Imperial College London]].

==Career==
Jones worked for a year for a company specialising in the design of laboratory equipment and then as a post-doctoral fellow at Imperial, where he worked on [[infrared spectroscopy]] and began his column for ''New Scientist''.<ref name="Times"/> In 1967, he took up a post as an assistant lecturer at the [[University of Strathclyde]]. After one year he moved to [[Runcorn]], Cheshire where he worked as a research scientist in spectroscopy for [[Imperial Chemical Industries]].<ref name="NYT"/> In 1974, he became the Sir James Knott Research Fellow at the [[Newcastle University|University of Newcastle upon Tyne]]. He then became an independent science consultant to industry providing ideas, [[brainstorming]] services, and scientific demonstrations for television.

Some of his Daedalus inventions proved practical; about one-fifth of them were seriously proposed or even patented by others.<ref name="Times"/> His most notable scientific contribution as Daedalus was possibly his 1966 prediction of hollow carbon molecules,<ref>{{cite journal
| journal = New Scientist
| issue = 32
| year = 1966
| pages = 245
| title = Hollow molecules
| last = Jones
| first = David E. H.
 }}</ref> before [[buckminsterfullerene]] was made,<ref name="JonesWasserman1993">{{cite journal|last1=Jones|first1=D. E. H.|last2=Wasserman|first2=E.|last3=Applewhite|first3=E. J.|last4=Kroto|first4=H. W.|last5=Iijima|first5=S.|last6=Haddon|first6=R. C.|last7=Pillinger|first7=C. T.|title=Dreams in a Charcoal Fire: Predictions about Giant Fullerenes and Graphite Nanotubes [and Discussion]|journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences|volume=343|issue=1667|year=1993|pages=9–18|issn=1364-503X|doi=10.1098/rsta.1993.0036|bibcode=1993RSPTA.343....9J|s2cid=120187894}}</ref> and long before its synthesizers won a Nobel prize for the discovery of [[fullerenes]].<ref>{{cite news |title= David Jones, British chemist and 'court jester in the palace of science,' dies at 79 |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=31 July 2017 |access-date=1 August 2017 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/obituaries/david-jones-british-chemist-and-court-jester-in-the-palace-of-science-dies-at-79/2017/07/31/8dfcb0c4-75fb-11e7-9eac-d56bd5568db8_story.html}}</ref> It is often claimed that the invention of [[3D printing]] was in 1984 by [[Chuck Hull]], but Jones in his Daedalus persona laid out the concept in ''New Scientist'' in 1974, 10 years earlier.<ref>{{Cite magazine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nvabM3KXNsUC&pg=PA80 |title=Ariadne |date=3 October 1974 |magazine=New Scientist |page=80 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200724194125/https://books.google.com/books?id=nvabM3KXNsUC&pg=PA80#v=onepage&q&f=false |archive-date=24 July 2020 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=9 November 2016 |title=Letter: 3D printing: you read it here first |url=https://www.newscientist.com/letter/mg23230991-100-1-editors-pick-3d-printing-you-read-it-here-first/ |url-status=live |access-date=2021-11-11 |website=New Scientist |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190817095138/https://www.newscientist.com/letter/mg23230991-100-1-editors-pick-3d-printing-you-read-it-here-first/ |archive-date=17 August 2019 }}</ref> He was an early proposer of a [[space elevator]] (1964) and of [[archaeoacoustics]] (1969).

Beyond Daedalus, in scientific circles he is known for his study of [[Bicycle and motorcycle dynamics|bicycle stability]],<ref name="jones">{{cite journal
| journal = Physics Today
| volume = 23
| issue = 4
| year = 1970
| pages = 34–40
| title = The stability of the bicycle
| last = Jones
| first = David E. H.
| url = https://www.phys.lsu.edu/faculty/gonzalez/Teaching/Phys7221/vol59no9p51_56.pdf| doi = 10.1063/1.3022064
| bibcode = 1970PhT....23d..34J }}</ref> his determination of [[arsenic]] in [[Napoleon]]'s wallpaper,<ref>{{citation |title=Arsenic in Napoleon's wallpaper |first1=David E. H. |last1= Jones |first2= Kenneth W. D. |last2= Ledingham |date=14 October 1982 |doi=10.1038/299626a0 |pmid=6750412 |journal=Nature |volume=299 |issue=5884 |pages=626–627 |bibcode =1982Natur.299..626J |s2cid=5378714 }}</ref> and for having designed and flown on the [[Space Shuttle]] a [[microgravity]] experiment<ref>{{citation |title=The Silicate Garden Reaction in Microgravity: A Fluid Interfacial Instability |first1=David E. H.  |last1= Jones |first2= Ulrich |last2= Walter |publisher=Elsevier |date=15 July 1988 |doi=10.1006/jcis.1998.5447 |pmid=9705766 |journal=Journal of Colloid and Interface Science |volume=203 |issue=2 |pages=286–293
|bibcode=1998JCIS..203..286J }}</ref> to grow a [[chemical garden]].<ref name="BargeCardoso2015">{{cite journal |last=Barge |first1=Laura M. |last2=Cardoso |first2=Silvana S. H. |last12=Mackay |first12=Alan L. |last13=Maselko |first13=Jerzy |last14=Pagano |first14=Jason J. |last15=Pantaleone |first15=J. |last16=Russell |first16=Michael J. |last17=Sainz-Díaz |first17=C. Ignacio |last18=Steinbock |first18=Oliver |last19=Stone |first19=David A. |last20=Tanimoto |first20=Yoshifumi |last21=Thomas |first21=Noreen L. |title=From Chemical Gardens to Chemobrionics |journal=Chemical Reviews |volume=115 |issue=16 |year=2015 |pages=8652–8703 |issn=0009-2665 |doi=10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00014 |pmid=26176351 |bibcode=2015ChRv..115.8652B |doi-access=free |hdl=20.500.11824/172 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

He is also known for his series of fake [[perpetual motion]] machines, one of which is in the ''[[Technisches Museum Wien]]''. In 2009, a documentary film about his work and inventions, ''Perpetual Motion Machine'',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://perpetualmotionmachinefilm.blogspot.co.nz/ |title=Website of Perpetual Motion Machine film |publisher=[[Blogspot]] |accessdate=9 May 2014}}</ref><!--<ref>[http://www.gallopingfilms.com/gf/2DocHumanInt2.html#Anchor-PMM Writeup of Perpetual Motion Machine film]</ref> --> was made and shown at the [[Newcastle Science Festival]] 2010.<ref>[https://cnr.lwlss.net/DavidJones Blog entry on film, with photographs]</ref>

He was known in Germany as a regular guest on the 1980s TV science quiz show ''Kopf um Kopf'' (''Head to Head''), presenting interesting physics experiments.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1ObdE9n3UF4 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/1ObdE9n3UF4 |archive-date=2021-12-21 |url-status=live |title=WDR – Kopf um Kopf – 1986, David Jones enters at 23:00 |date=6 January 2012 |via=YouTube |accessdate=10 May 2014}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

==Personal life==

In 1972, he married Jane Burgess. The marriage lasted a year, and he later had a long relationship with the artist Naomi Hunt.<ref name="Times"/>

He died in 2017 from prostate cancer.<ref name="Telegraph-obit">{{cite news|title=David Jones, 'Daedalus', the scientific joker – obituary|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/obituaries/2017/07/27/david-jones-daedalus-scientific-joker-obituary/|accessdate=29 July 2017|work=[[Telegraph Media Group|The Telegraph]]|date=27 July 2017}}</ref><ref name="NYT"/>
